_schema.about: Rotation templates: alternatives built from the farmer's CURRENT rotation. Read by the backend, replayed through 2005-2025 and scored. Crop timing lives in data/crops/crops.csv; bare months are computed by the backend, not entered here.
_schema.name: shown on the card; {current} is replaced by the farmer's rotation, e.g. 'Corn / Soybean'
_schema.idea: one of: cover_crop | small_grain | legume | perennial | drought_tolerant
_schema.steps: the sequence, one entry per block of years. {"use_current": true} = the farmer's current rotation (optionally with "cover_crop" added to every year). Otherwise {"main_crop": crop_id, "cover_crop": crop_id or null, "years": n}. crop_ids must exist in crops.csv
_schema.requires: constraint ids the farmer must have, matching the frontend checkboxes: irrigation | hay_equipment (ask before adding new ones)
_schema.market_requirements: plain-text market needs, e.g. 'Local hay buyer or own livestock'
_schema.why: one plain sentence: the agronomic idea behind this template
_schema.benefits: general benefits (the backend adds field-specific ones with numbers)
_schema.risks_for_local_review: things a local agronomist/farmer should check
_schema.data_gaps: what we could not verify or do not model

templates.name: {current} + cereal rye cover
templates.market_requirements: No separate grain market is required; the farmer needs access to cereal rye seed and a suitable seeding and termination method.
templates.why: Adding cereal rye as a winter cover crop keeps living roots and protective residue on the field between cash crops.
benefits: Can reduce soil erosion by maintaining ground cover.
Can capture residual nutrients that might otherwise be lost during the off-season.
Can suppress some weeds and increase the amount of plant residue returned to the soil.
Can be added without replacing the farmer's existing cash-crop sequence.
risks_for_local_review: Cereal rye must be established early enough after harvest to produce useful growth before winter.
Terminate rye at least 10 days before planting corn; Iowa State commonly recommends a 10-14 day interval.
Late termination can increase competition for water and nitrogen and may increase corn seedling disease risk.
Check herbicide choice, application timing, weather, and crop-insurance requirements locally.
data_gaps: The model does not estimate actual rye biomass or nitrogen immobilization.
The model does not determine the best termination date from field conditions.
Cover-crop establishment success depends on harvest date, rainfall, and seeding method.

sources.title: Iowa State Extension - Terminating cover crops ahead of corn
Iowa State Extension - Cereal Rye Cover Crops, Allelopathy and Corn
Iowa State Extension - Iowa Cover Crop Recipe: Post Corn, Going to Soybean

templates.name: {current} / Winter wheat + red clover
templates.market_requirements: A local buyer or other reliable use for winter wheat grain is needed; confirm access to suitable planting and harvesting equipment.
templates.why: Introducing winter wheat with red clover adds a small grain and a legume phase to diversify the conventional corn-soybean sequence.
benefits: Adds a different crop family and growing season to the rotation.
Can provide additional periods of soil cover and living roots.
Red clover can contribute biologically fixed nitrogen when successfully established.
A different harvest window can spread fieldwork across the season.
Can create an opportunity for another crop or cover crop after wheat harvest.
risks_for_local_review: Confirm that winter wheat is suitable for the field's location, variety, planting date, and winter conditions.
Red clover establishment can be poor if seeding conditions or moisture are unsuitable.
Confirm local grain buyers, expected prices, storage, and harvesting arrangements before planting.
Check wheat disease, weed, and residue-management risks with a local agronomist.
data_gaps: The model does not predict wheat or red clover yield or farm profitability.
The model does not estimate the nitrogen contribution from red clover.
Actual winter survival and red clover establishment depend on local weather and management.

sources.title: USDA NRCS - Whole Farm Conservation Best Practices Manual
USDA NRCS and Iowa State Extension - Winter Wheat Cover Crop Fact Sheet for Iowa

templates.name: {current} / 2 years alfalfa
templates.market_requirements: A reliable local hay buyer, livestock operation, or custom hay-harvesting service is needed.
templates.why: Adding a two-year alfalfa phase introduces a perennial legume with continuous soil cover and potential nitrogen benefits for following crops.
benefits: Perennial ground cover can reduce erosion during the alfalfa phase.
Alfalfa fixes atmospheric nitrogen through its association with soil bacteria.
Alfalfa can improve soil organic matter and reduce nitrate leaching.
The crop following a successfully managed alfalfa stand may benefit from residual nitrogen.
A hay phase diversifies farm production beyond annual grain crops.
risks_for_local_review: Confirm that the field has suitable drainage, soil pH, and conditions for establishing alfalfa.
A successful stand requires appropriate establishment, cutting, and weed management.
The farmer needs hay harvesting equipment or access to a reliable custom operator.
Check local hay demand, storage capacity, and transport costs.
Alfalfa termination must be managed carefully to prevent regrowth and competition with the next crop.
data_gaps: The model does not estimate hay yield, quality, or market price.
The model does not calculate the field-specific nitrogen credit after alfalfa.
The model does not simulate stand establishment, cutting schedules, or stand persistence.

sources.title: Clean Water Iowa - Extended Crop Rotation

templates.name: Sorghum / Soybean
templates.market_requirements: Confirm a local grain buyer, suitable seed availability, and harvesting arrangements for sorghum before recommending this rotation.
templates.why: Replacing a corn phase with sorghum introduces a warm-season grain that can be a useful alternative where water availability limits corn production.
benefits: Sorghum can maintain grain production under some moisture-limited conditions where corn performance declines.
Introduces a different crop species into the rotation.
Can diversify production and reduce dependence on a corn-only summer grain phase.
Soybean provides a following legume crop in the sequence.
risks_for_local_review: Sorghum is not drought-proof and can still use substantial soil moisture.
Check local growing-season length, planting temperature, maturity, and frost risk.
Confirm that a suitable sorghum market and harvesting infrastructure exist.
Sorghum residue can temporarily tie up nitrogen during decomposition.
Check whether the sequence fits local weed, pest, and disease management.
data_gaps: The model does not establish that sorghum is economically viable for every Iowa farm.
The model does not predict sorghum grain yield, harvest moisture, or local market price.
Sorghum water-use response depends on variety, soil, weather, and management.
The rotation comparison should not be interpreted as a guarantee of improved drought performance.
